summary: A 1975 comment on the IMP and host protocol changes of RFC 687 and RFC 690, proposing a solution to the problem of the combined length of the IMP and host leaders. See also RFC 696.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 692 comments on proposed changes to the IMP/Host protocol. It suggests a different IMP header length and a message that would provide hosts with names and network addresses.

questions: comments on imp host protocol changes
what is the imp host protocol
what is the imp host leader length problem
subtitle: A proposal to keep revised IMP and Host leaders at a workable combined length.

tldr.problem: Changes discussed in RFC 687 and RFC 690 would make the combined IMP and Host leaders 120 bits, a length that does not fit both 8-bit and 36-bit units.
tldr.mechanism: Wolfe proposes a 104-bit IMP leader, with rules for its last 8 bits and irregular messages. He also suggests a message that gives hosts a table of host names and network addresses.
tldr.outcome: This RFC is a comment proposing alternatives, not a specification. It updates RFC 690, according to the unit metadata.

today: RFC 692 updates RFC 690; the unit metadata lists its status as Unknown and names no later RFC that updates or replaces it. The document is a comment proposing changes to the IMP/Host protocol.

sections.title: The Combined Leader Length
sections.content:
Wolfe considers the changes in RFC 687 and the comments in RFC 690 broadly reasonable. He identifies a problem in the combined IMP and Host leaders: their proposed total length of 120 bits is not a multiple of both 8 and 36 bits.

One suggested fix was to add 24 bits to the Host leader, making the combined length 144 bits. Wolfe says this would require the IMP to insert or remove those bits when translating between old and new formats.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposed headers add up to a length that does not fit both systems' data units. Making the Host header longer would force the IMP to change the header when translating it.

sections.title: A Different IMP Leader Length
sections.content:
Wolfe prefers an IMP leader of 104 bits instead of 80. Although 104 is not a multiple of an IMP word, he says it can work if the last 8 bits carry no information and the network is not required to preserve or return them.

For messages other than type zero, which the RFC calls irregular messages, the IMP may send 96, 104 or 112 bits of data at its convenience. The RFC also says either 96 or 112 bits could be used as the new leader length for irregular messages. Wolfe argues that changing the IMP program would be faster and cheaper than requiring changes in all hosts.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposal changes the IMP header and treats its last 8 bits as unused. For certain messages, the IMP can choose among three data lengths.

sections.title: A Message for Host Names and Addresses
sections.content:
Wolfe also proposes a new IMP-to-Host message containing a table of host names and network addresses. The network could send the table after each interface reset, or send it in response to a new request from a host.

The proposal is an additional suggestion in this comment on protocol changes. It does not specify the full message format or define a complete implementation procedure.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposed message would give a computer a list matching host names to network addresses. The network could send it after a reset or when the computer asks.
